mcqs.question: What should actually determine whether a record moves from hot to warm to cold storage?
options: The record's file format
How old the record is in calendar days, regardless of anything else
Its actual access pattern — how often and how urgently it's read — not age alone
Which team originally created the record
mcqs.explanation: Access pattern is the real signal — age alone can be misleading, since some old data stays frequently accessed and some new data goes cold quickly. File format and the owning team aren't relevant to the hot/warm/cold decision.

mcqs.question: A team wants to set the boundary between their hot and warm storage tiers. What does the tiered-storage comparison recommend?
options: Always use exactly 30 days as the boundary, since it's an industry standard
Pick whichever boundary requires the least code change
Copy whatever boundary a competitor uses
Measure actual access frequency by age and set the boundary where real usage drops off
mcqs.explanation: The comparison explicitly recommends measuring real access frequency rather than guessing or defaulting to a round number. There's no universal 30-day standard, least-code-change isn't a sound basis for a cost/latency trade-off, and copying a competitor ignores your own actual access pattern.

mcqs.question: A system stores financial transaction records that regulations require keeping for 7 years, even though they're rarely queried after 90 days. What's the correct storage approach?
options: Set a 90-day TTL and delete the data once queries stop, since it's not commercially needed
Keep all 7 years of data on hot storage regardless of cost, to be safe
Move the data to cold/cheap storage after it goes unused, but never delete it before the mandated 7-year period
Delete the data immediately since regulatory data doesn't belong in production systems
mcqs.explanation: Compliance-driven retention still allows moving data to cheaper storage as it goes cold, but forbids deleting it before the legally mandated period regardless of query frequency. TTL-based deletion at 90 days would violate the requirement, and keeping everything on expensive hot storage wastes money without a commercial justification.

mcqs.question: A team sets a 90-day TTL on a table, assuming "nothing reads data that old anyway." Months later, an annual reconciliation job breaks. What was the mistake?
options: The TTL feature itself is broken and needs a vendor patch
Setting the TTL without first auditing every consumer of the data, including infrequent ones like annual jobs
TTLs should never be used on any table under any circumstances
The reconciliation job should have been deleted along with the old data
mcqs.explanation: The pitfall is exactly this: assuming no one needs old data without checking infrequent consumers like annual or rarely-triggered jobs. TTL functionality isn't at fault here, TTLs are useful when scoped correctly, and deleting the reconciliation job isn't a fix for a data-availability mistake.

mcqs.question: A team moves 90-day-old data to a cold archive tier to cut storage costs, but a support tool ends up querying that data weekly. What's the risk?
options: Retrieval fees and latency from the cold tier can erode or reverse the storage savings, and users experience multi-hour waits for data expected instantly
Nothing — cold storage always costs less than hot storage no matter how often it's accessed
Cold storage tiers automatically re-promote frequently accessed data to hot storage at no cost
The archive tier will simply reject queries after the first retrieval
mcqs.explanation: Cold tiers trade cheap storage for expensive, slow retrieval, so unexpectedly frequent access can make the total cost, and user experience, worse than staying hot. Most archive tiers don't auto-promote data for free, and they don't reject repeated queries outright, they just charge and delay each one.
